Michael Moritz on the Time profile that ended his relationship with Steve Jobs, and whether he was ever in awe of him.

"Steve was convinced that he was going to be named Man of the Year, even though nobody had told him that. 

But worst of all, the profile, which he hated for very good reason, and I was appalled by for different reasons, severed my relationship with Steve. 

Back then at Time, these things went through an editorial combine harvester. 

So what came out in the bale at the end probably didn't resemble very much of the straw that got fed in. And so the whole tone of the piece was malicious and nasty and underhanded. 

Sadly, as a result of that, really never repaired the relationship with Steve.

Were you in awe of him? 

No.

I respected him. I admired him tremendously. But I knew some of the darker shades of him, which made it difficult to hold him up as an object of unalloyed admiration. But he's a heroic figure, obviously."

Michael joined Sequoia in 1986 and co-led the firm with Doug Leone (@dougleone) from 1995 to 2012. His investments include Google, Yahoo, PayPal, and Stripe.

One thing I didn't focus on enough in my last post about @TrezuApp is the lack of commercial confidentiality in crypto.

Once someone links a wallet to your company, they can start estimating your budgets, salaries, contractor payments, or even how much runway you have left.

That can give contractors leverage in negotiations and competitors insight into how your business operates.

Essentially, Trezu lets teams hold crypto, pay employees and contractors, swap tokens, and manage payment approvals in one place, with the option to keep your finances private.

Governance stays public and verifiable. Finances stay private.

With Confidential Treasuries, anyone can see the multisig members and that a vote took place, but they can't see how much money the treasury holds or who the team is paying.

The confidential treasury runs on a private shard on @NEARProtocol, letting teams:

→ Keep treasury balances private
→ Keep payment proposals visible only to the team
→ Pay contractors in batches with multisig approvals

And when you pay a contractor’s public wallet, the money arrives from a generic NEAR Intents address. Someone checking that wallet would see a transfer from a smart contract, without a direct public link back to your company’s treasury.

So if you’re managing company funds onchain, you can create a confidential treasury for free: https://t.co/IlP1eO86JE

Do you like $INTC ?

I believe Intel has had several significant positive developments over the past month. The stock appears to have bottomed around $85 and now trades near $97.

Yesterday, I opened the following trade, which expires on November 20:

Buy one $95 call.
Sell three $130 calls.
Sell one $80 put.

The maximum profit is around $130, meaning Intel would need to rise approximately 33% by November 20. On the downside, I only start losing if Intel falls more than 20%, at which point I would be assigned the shares at $80. On the upside, the trade remains profitable unless Intel rises more than approximately 51% from that point you start loosing money.

My logic is as follows: 

1) We are entering a period of weak seasonality, which is usually a difficult time for the stock market. That is one reason I feel comfortable selling the three $130 calls, I intentionally want to waste time.

2) On the other hand, Intel has had several positive developments recently. That is why I also feel comfortable selling the $80 put.

That is the basic logic behind the trade: I am positive on Intel, but I am not expecting an extreme move higher by November 20. The sweet spot is a ~35% rise in the next 66 days, with the maximum profit around $130.

You could also view this trade as an add-on to an existing Intel position. Let’s say Intel currently represents 5% of your portfolio. If the stock rises “only” to $130, you will make money on both the options and the stock. If it rises 50% to $150, you will still be very happy because of the profit on your shares, despite not making money on the options trade.

If Intel falls to $80, perhaps that is a price at which you would feel comfortable doubling your position. You receive additional shares at a price you like and continue holding them because you believe Intel should perform well over the long term.

Remember, this is just an idea, not a recommendation. You might want to choose different strikes or expiration.

Biotech Contemplation

I recently wrote that our biotech expert likes $IONS. But the more time I spend around biotech, the harder it becomes for me to recommend companies with major Phase 3 trials ahead of them.

Unless you run a dedicated biotech fund, there are several problems.

You can wake up one morning and discover that another company’s similar drug has failed. Suddenly, your stock is down 10%, 20%, or even 30% because of a negative read-through, without giving you any chance to react.

That kind of risk also limits how large the position can be. And the more I think about it, the more I believe that owning a stock at just 1% or 2% of your portfolio is mostly a waste of time. But if the stock can fall 30% overnight because of another company’s trial, it is very difficult to build a meaningful position.

It is true that we have had some big biotech winners. But I also see the losers, and more importantly, I see how difficult it is to put serious money into these companies while controlling the risk.

Going forward, I will still publish ideas from our biotech expert and I will mention they come from our biotech expert because the medicine is interesting and his research is valuable. But my own focus will be mainly on companies I research myself and reach my own conclusions on, such as $URGN after they passed their phase 3 and $WGS.

I will generally avoid companies like $IONS and other biotech names I have discussed in the past, unless they are already profitable, generating real cash, and do not have major Phase 3 risks hanging over them.

We recently published an article on how we’re building our own internal AI infrastructure for VC here at Draper. Custom workflows to help our team gather information faster, so they can get back to the true human work in VC: meeting with and being present with founders.

In 1985, I built my deal flow by knocking on the doors of the ten or so venture capitalists that existed and asking them to send me the deals they were declining. I needed to build knowledge so I could build judgment.

Forty years later, the team at Draper Associates built something I could only have dreamed of back then:

-One centralized database that holds a singular record per company that has all our internal data as well as enriched data from outside verified sources like Harmonic

-A machine learning model, trained on 40+ years of successes and passes, that reads the hundreds of deals we get every week and surfaces the best fits directly to the investment team

-A brief on every meeting before we walk in

-Warm intros drafted from a network of 15,000+ contacts

-Answers to any question from our own records in plain English across 400+ portfolio companies (and an extra info assist from our Harmonic API)

The AI/ML infrastructure handles the routine work, but judgment remains human: sitting across from a founder, recognizing a missionary, making the call while the idea still sounds crazy.

Now there are more hours for exactly that.
